analysis.one_liner: Repeals federal construction wage floors, curbs union enforcement, opens public land and waters to drilling, and rolls back regulations.
analysis.headline: A sweeping package of labor, regulatory, and energy rollbacks sponsored by Rep. Steve Scalise with 53 Republican cosponsors was referred to 13 House committees and died without ever receiving a vote when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This was a catch-all bill that rolled together labor, regulatory, and energy changes. It would have repealed the Davis-Bacon Act, which requires federally funded construction projects to pay the local prevailing wage; stripped the National Labor Relations Board of its power to prosecute employers for unfair labor practices; required Congress to approve every major federal rule before it could take effect; and opened the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, the Atlantic and Pacific outer continental shelf, and other federal land and waters to oil and gas drilling, while blocking EPA climate rules and approving the Keystone XL pipeline without a presidential permit. It was referred to 13 committees, none acted, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies gain mandated offshore lease sales, new access to the Arctic refuge and the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska, faster drilling permits with automatic approval if the government misses deadlines, freedom from federal fracking rules, and a Keystone XL approval that bypasses the president. Coal companies gain the end of EPA climate authority and looser coal ash and mining rules. Federal construction contractors gain the right to pay below prevailing wages. Private equity firms, merger brokers, and community banks gain exemptions from SEC registration and consumer-finance rules. Employers facing union drives gain because the NLRB could no longer prosecute unfair labor practices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil, gas, and coal companies and federal contractors

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Davis-Bacon Act, letting contractors on federally funded construction pay below the local prevailing wage.

Requires lease sales covering at least half the unleased acreage in the most promising offshore planning areas, opens the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge Coastal Plain to leasing, and approves the Keystone XL pipeline without a presidential permit.
Speeds drilling permits on federal land by deeming applications approved if the Interior Department misses a 60-day deadline, and blocks federal fracking rules wherever a state has its own.

Imposes cost-benefit analysis on all new rules, requires periodic sunset reviews of existing rules, gives small businesses a six-month grace period before regulatory penalties, and requires Congress to approve major rules before they take effect.
Exempts private equity fund advisers and merger-and-acquisition brokers from SEC registration and gives community banks relief from escrow, privacy-notice, and accounting rules.

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federally funded projects could see pay fall without the Davis-Bacon prevailing wage. Workers relying on the NLRB to enforce labor rights would have to file their own federal lawsuits. The public bears expanded drilling in the Arctic refuge and offshore waters with expedited review, weaker coal ash and mining rules, the removal of EPA climate authority, and a system in which major federal rules die unless Congress affirmatively approves them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Construction workers, union members, and the public

drawbacks.text: Repealing Davis-Bacon would let contractors on federally funded construction pay less than the locally prevailing wage, directly cutting pay for construction workers.

Stripping the NLRB's power to issue and prosecute complaints would leave workers alleging illegal employer conduct to bring their own federal lawsuits, without the Board's investigatory and enforcement machinery.

State programs for developing energy on federal land would be exempt from the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, and judicial review, cutting communities and courts out of decisions about drilling near them.
Excluding greenhouse gases from the definition of an air pollutant and banning use of the social cost of carbon would end federal climate regulation under the Clean Air Act.

Requiring Congress to affirmatively approve every major federal rule — with rules dying automatically after 70 legislative days without approval — would make it far harder for any agency to issue significant health, safety, or environmental protections.

The strongest good-faith case for the bill is that prevailing-wage mandates, permitting delays, and compliance paperwork raise costs for contractors, small businesses, and ultimately taxpayers and consumers; the grace period and cost-benefit provisions respond to that concern, though at the price of delayed enforcement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundles some real, modest relief for small businesses and community banks — a six-month grace period before regulatory penalties, simpler merger paperwork, and lighter compliance rules — with far larger gains for fossil fuel and financial interests. Its labor provisions would cut pay on federally funded construction jobs and leave workers to enforce labor law through their own lawsuits. Its energy and environmental provisions would open protected lands and waters to drilling while cutting courts, states' environmental review, and EPA climate authority out of the process. The benefits would flow to concentrated industries; the costs — lower wages, weaker workplace rights, and long-term climate and environmental damage — would be spread across the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2014, referred to 13 House committees and then to about a dozen subcommittees, none of which ever reported it, and it expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Scalise introduced the bill on March 26, 2014, with 30 original cosponsors.
The same day, the House referred it to 13 standing committees, from Natural Resources and Budget to Ways and Means and Financial Services.
Between late March and mid-June 2014 it was further referred to about 18 subcommittees covering aviation, energy, public lands, regulatory reform, workforce protections, and other subjects.
It gathered 53 cosponsors, all Republicans, but no committee ever reported it, no vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, federal construction workers kept prevailing-wage protections, unions kept the NLRB as an enforcer, and oil, gas, and coal companies gained no new access to protected lands, waters, or relief from climate rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Construction workers, unions, and environmental protections

for.name: Rep. Steve Scalise
for.what_they_did: Introduced the omnibus bill on March 26, 2014.

against.name: Chairs of the 13 referred House committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in March 2014 and never reported it out of committee or scheduled a markup before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 53 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never reached a floor vote where party splits could be measured.

industries.note: The bill mandates offshore lease sales, opens the Arctic refuge and National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska to drilling, deems drilling permits approved on deadlines, blocks federal fracking rules, and approves Keystone XL without a presidential permit. Its gains come from expanded access to public lands and waters and reduced environmental review.

It excludes greenhouse gases from the Clean Air Act, lets states run coal ash permit programs, reinstates the 2008 stream buffer rule and blocks a stricter one, and relaxes emission limits for coal-refuse plants. The relief comes by removing pollution and climate protections the public currently has.
Repealing Davis-Bacon lets them pay below the locally prevailing wage on federally financed projects, lowering their labor costs directly at construction workers' expense.

Gutting the NLRB's power to issue and prosecute complaints and limiting its rulemaking to internal functions removes the main government enforcer of workers' organizing and bargaining rights; disputes would shift to private lawsuits by individual workers.

industries.industry: Private equity firms and securities brokers
industries.note: Exemptions from Investment Advisers Act registration for private equity advisers and from Securities Exchange Act registration for M&A brokers reduce federal oversight of firms managing pooled investor money.

industries.industry: Community banks and small mortgage servicers
industries.note: Relief from escrow requirements, annual privacy notices, Sarbanes-Oxley internal-control audits, and appraisal thresholds eases compliance costs at smaller institutions; some of this genuinely reduces burdens on local lenders, though some consumer protections are loosened too.
